title: Critical path analysis
blurb: State the purpose of critical path analysis: the minimum duration, the activities to watch, where the flexibility is and how to shorten.
question: The sponsor of a new website asks two things: what is the earliest the site can launch, and which tasks must the team watch most closely to protect that date? Which technique answers both questions?

teach.h: The longest path sets the shortest time
teach.body: Draw every activity and its dependencies as a network, and you get several paths from start to finish. The critical path is the LONGEST sequence of dependent activities through that network. Because nothing can finish until that chain is done, its length is the SHORTEST possible duration for the whole project. Shorter paths run alongside it with time to spare.

teach.caption: Requirements, design, build and test form the critical path. Content and hosting can slip a little without moving the launch.
Req = Requirements. The longest path decides the launch date. You will not be asked to calculate this in the PFQ: just know what it means.

teach.body: Critical path analysis establishes the minimum project duration, identifies the critical activities that need the closest control, shows the float (flexibility) on every other activity, and supports decisions about shortening the schedule. In plain English: it tells you how fast you can go, what you must not let slip, where you have breathing space and where extra effort would actually help.

teach.h: Four things critical path analysis tells you

children.label: Where to shorten
children.sub: only critical work moves the end

teach.body: If Build overruns by a week, the launch slips a week, because Build has no float. If Write content overruns by a week, nothing happens to the launch: it had three weeks of float. And if the sponsor wants an earlier launch, adding writers is pointless; effort must go into shortening Requirements, Design, Build or Test. That is critical path analysis doing its job.

items: Re-check the critical path whenever progress is updated: it can change.
A non-critical activity that slips past its float becomes critical.
Shortening the critical path can make another path the new longest one.
Report the critical activities to the sponsor, as they drive the end date.

teach.text: The critical path is the LONGEST path, and it gives the SHORTEST possible duration. 'Critical' means time-critical (zero float), not 'most important', 'most expensive' or 'highest risk'. Don't confuse it with critical CHAIN, a related, resource-focused technique that uses buffers.

items: Critical path: the longest sequence of dependent activities from start to finish.
It sets the shortest possible project duration.
Critical activities have zero total float: any delay to them delays the end date.
Purpose: minimum duration, activities to control closely, float elsewhere, decisions on shortening.
The critical path can change as the project progresses.

summary: You can now state the purpose of critical path analysis: to find the minimum project duration, identify the zero-float activities that need closest control, reveal float elsewhere and guide decisions on shortening the schedule. You also know that the critical path is the longest path and can change.

A.q: What does the critical path determine?
options: The cheapest way of delivering the work
The activities with the highest risk
The furthest any activity may be late
A.why: Nothing can finish until the longest chain of dependent activities is complete, so the critical path sets the minimum duration.

whyNot.1: Critical path analysis is about time, not finding the cheapest approach.
whyNot.2: 'Critical' means zero float, not highest risk; risk is assessed separately.
whyNot.3: How far a non-critical activity may slip is its float, which is a by-product, not what the critical path determines.

A.q: Complete the statement: the critical path is the ______ sequence of dependent activities from the start to the end of the project.
A.why: The critical path is the longest path through the network, and so it determines the shortest possible duration.

whyNot.0: The shortest path has the most float; it is not critical.
whyNot.2: Cost plays no part in defining the critical path.
whyNot.3: Risk level does not define the critical path; time does.

A.q: How much total float do activities on the critical path have?
A.why: Critical activities have zero total float, so any delay to them delays the project end date.

whyNot.0: Activities on shorter paths have the most float, not critical ones.
whyNot.1: Float is not linked to an activity's own duration.
whyNot.3: Float comes from the network logic, not from a sponsor's decision.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following are purposes of critical path analysis?
1. Establish the minimum project duration
2. Calculate the project's net present value
3. Identify the activities needing closest control
4. Select suppliers for the work
B.why: Critical path analysis finds the minimum duration and the critical activities that need closest control.

whyNot.0: Net present value is an investment appraisal measure in the business case.
whyNot.1: Neither NPV nor supplier selection is a purpose of critical path analysis.
whyNot.2: Supplier selection belongs to the procurement strategy, not critical path analysis.

B.q: On a website project, Build is critical and Write content has three weeks of float. Both run one week late. What is the most likely effect on the launch?
options: It is not affected at all
It slips because of the content
It slips because of the build
It comes forward by a week
B.why: Build has zero float, so its delay moves the launch. The content delay is absorbed by its float.

whyNot.0: A critical activity is late, so the launch is affected.
whyNot.1: Write content had three weeks of float, so a one-week delay is absorbed.
whyNot.3: Delays never bring an end date forward.

B.q: A sponsor wants the project finished earlier. Where does critical path analysis say the effort to shorten the schedule should go?
options: Activities that have the most float
B.why: Only shortening critical activities can bring the end date forward; shortening activities with float just adds more float.

whyNot.0: Shortening an activity with float does not move the end date.
whyNot.2: Cost does not decide which activities drive the duration.
whyNot.3: Who owns an activity doesn't make it critical; zero float does.

C.q: A trainee lists what critical path analysis is for. Which item on the list is wrong?
C.why: Ranking risks by impact is part of risk assessment. The other three are genuine purposes of critical path analysis.

whyNot.0: Revealing float on non-critical activities is a purpose of the analysis.
whyNot.1: Establishing the minimum project duration is its main purpose.
whyNot.2: Identifying critical activities that need closest control is a purpose.

C.q: A non-critical activity slips by more than its total float. What happens?
options: It becomes critical and the end slips
Its float grows to absorb the delay
The critical path cannot be affected
The project end date moves earlier
C.why: Once the delay exceeds its float, the activity now drives the end date: it has joined (or become) the critical path, and the project finishes later.

whyNot.1: Float is fixed by the network logic; it doesn't grow to absorb a delay.
whyNot.2: The critical path can change when a non-critical activity slips beyond its float.
whyNot.3: A delay can never bring the end date forward.

C.q: Which statement about the word 'critical' in critical path analysis is correct?
options: It means the activity carries most risk
It means the sponsor must approve it
It means a delay to it delays the end
It means the activity costs the most
C.why: 'Critical' is about time: a critical activity has zero float, so delaying it delays the project end date.

whyNot.0: A critical activity may be low risk; risk is assessed separately.
whyNot.1: Sponsor approval has nothing to do with whether an activity is critical.
whyNot.3: Cost does not determine whether an activity is on the critical path.

reteach.title: Think of getting the family out of the door
reteach.question: Everyone must be in the car by 8:30. One child takes 40 minutes to get ready; the others take 15. Whose routine decides when you can leave?

blocks.body: Breakfast, then shower, then hair-drying takes 40 minutes in a row. Packing the bags and finding shoes takes 15. However quickly the rest of you move, you leave when the longest chain is done. That chain is the critical path. The others have spare minutes (float). Rushing the bag-packer won't get you out sooner; speeding up the 40-minute routine will.

blocks.text: If the hairdryer breaks and drying takes ten minutes longer, you leave ten minutes late. If packing takes ten minutes longer, you still leave on time. That's the difference between zero float and float.

explain.body: The project cannot finish until its longest chain of dependent activities is done. So the longest path gives the shortest possible duration: the earliest end date you can promise.

test.q: Why does the LONGEST path through a network set the project's duration?
options: It is where most of the risks sit
It is the path the sponsor chooses
It has the most expensive tasks
All shorter paths finish within it
test.why: Shorter paths finish within the time the longest one takes, so the longest path decides when the project can end.

whyNot.0: Risk is not what makes a path long.
whyNot.1: The sponsor doesn't choose the critical path; the logic and durations do.
whyNot.2: Cost has no bearing on path length.

explain.body: Every activity on the critical path has zero total float. Delay one by a day and the whole project finishes a day later, unless the time is recovered elsewhere on the path. These are the activities to control most closely.

test.q: An activity on the critical path is delayed by a day and nothing is recovered. What happens to the end date?
options: It slips only if over budget
test.why: Critical activities have zero float, so the delay passes straight through to the end date.

whyNot.0: With zero float there is nothing to absorb the delay.
whyNot.1: A delay cannot move the end date earlier.
whyNot.3: Budget has nothing to do with whether time slips.

explain.body: Activities off the critical path have float: they can start late or run long, up to a limit, without moving the end date. Knowing where float exists tells the PM where there is flexibility to move work or people.

test.q: What does critical path analysis reveal about activities that are NOT on the critical path?
options: They can be removed from the scope
They have float, so some flexibility
They have no dependencies at all
test.why: Non-critical activities have float, which shows the PM where there is flexibility in the schedule.

whyNot.0: Being non-critical doesn't make work unnecessary.
whyNot.2: Closest monitoring is for critical activities.

explain.body: To finish earlier you must shorten critical activities, for example by adding resources or overlapping work. Shortening an activity with float only adds more float. And once the critical path shortens, another path may become the longest.

test.q: Shortening which activity could bring the project end date forward?
test.why: Only critical activities drive the end date, so only shortening them can move it earlier.

whyNot.1: Shortening an activity with float only increases its float.
whyNot.2: Most activities have float and won't move the end date.
whyNot.3: A milestone has zero duration, so there is nothing to shorten.
